theory.question: When does a single-node database stop being enough and you need sharding — with concrete capacity numbers for PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis, and DynamoDB
theory.answer:
Shard when data volume or write throughput exceeds what one node can store or process; if reads are the bottleneck, replication alone may suffice.

PostgreSQL (single node, no external sharding layer):
- Storage ceiling on managed Postgres is large but finite — AWS RDS PostgreSQL supports up to 64 TiB per instance; io2 storage can reach 256,000 provisioned IOPS and up to 16,000 MiB/s throughput on the largest configurations.
- Practical trigger is earlier: when the working set no longer fits RAM, write-heavy traffic saturates CPU/WAL/disk IOPS, or maintenance (vacuum, index builds, backups) becomes operationally risky. Vanilla PostgreSQL has no built-in horizontal sharding — you add Citus, Vitess, or application-level sharding when vertical scaling stops helping.

MongoDB (replica set → sharded cluster):
- MongoDB guidance: plan sharding when a collection approaches ~2–3 TB, or when a large instance (e.g., Atlas M60 with 4 TB disk) sits at 60–70% CPU/RAM/storage utilization for sustained periods.
- High sustained write throughput on a single primary is another signal — the same capacity rule applies: one leader can become the bottleneck even if total cluster storage is fine.

Redis (in-memory, cluster sharding):
- Data must fit in RAM on the nodes serving it (unless using tiered/flash extensions). Set `maxmemory` to ~70–80% of host RAM — e.g., ~22–26 GB on a 32 GB host, ~45–51 GB on 64 GB, ~90–102 GB on 128 GB; AWS ElastiCache's largest single node (cache.r7g.16xlarge) offers up to 512 GiB.
- A single open-source Redis process is single-threaded for commands — typical throughput is on the order of tens of thousands to low hundreds of thousands of ops/sec depending on value size and pipelining; Redis Enterprise benchmarks show ~5M ops/sec per large node with many shards. Shard when one node's memory (often before a ~64–128 GB working set on OSS Redis) or command throughput is saturated.

Cross-cutting book thresholds useful in design reviews:
- HBase auto-splits a region at ~10 GB by default, or when write throughput stays above a configured threshold.
- Fixed-shard designs (Citus, Riak, Elasticsearch) often pre-create hundreds or thousands of logical shards — e.g., 1,000 shards on 10 nodes (100 per node) — so node add/remove moves whole shards, not individual keys.

Sources: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/CHAP_Storage.html , https://www.mongodb.com/resources/products/capabilities/sharding , https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/rs/databases/memory-performance/ , https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/bp-partition-key-design.html

theory.question: Pros and cons of using sharding for multitenant SaaS (one shard per tenant vs several tenants per shard)
theory.answer:
Multitenant sharding trades operational isolation and compliance convenience against overhead and cross-tenant feature cost.

A SaaS tenant is a naturally separate dataset, such as one business in an email-marketing service. A large tenant can receive a dedicated shard while several small tenants share one shard.

Recommendation pattern: shard-by-tenant for large enterprise customers with strict isolation/residency needs; pool small tenants on shared shards with a tenant ID in every partition key; plan tenant migration tooling early.

Comment: AWS cell-based architecture whitepaper and Citus schema-based sharding are production implementations of this model.

theory.question: Key-range sharding: how it works, when to choose it, and how rebalancing happens
theory.answer:
Key-range sharding assigns each shard a contiguous interval of partition keys — like encyclopedia volumes sorted by title.

Boundaries may be manual (Vitess) or automatic (Bigtable/HBase, MongoDB range sharding, CockroachDB, FoundationDB). Ranges are not necessarily equal width — volume 12 may cover T–Z — so boundaries adapt to keep shards roughly even.

Choose key-range when:
- You need range queries on the partition key (time-series, lexicographic browsing).
- You can structure the key so related reads cluster without creating write hot spots (prefix sensor ID before timestamp).

Comment: Monotonic timestamp keys are a classic footgun — App Engine and HBase documentation describes the same risk.

theory.question: Hash-modulo sharding (`hash(key) % N`): mechanism and why changing node count is painful
theory.answer:
Hash-modulo sharding computes `hash(key) % N` and sends the key to that numbered shard. It is simple, deterministic, and usually spreads well-behaved keys evenly when the hash function is stable.

The problem is that `N` participates in every placement decision. Changing from eight shards to nine changes the remainder for most hashes, so most records move even though capacity increased by only one ninth. During that migration, clients need a transition map, dual reads or writes, and a way to reconcile requests that race with movement. A partial rollout can otherwise lose or duplicate data.

Use modulo only when the logical shard count is fixed and physical nodes can own several logical shards. If the number of placement buckets itself must grow, prefer consistent hashing, rendezvous hashing, or dynamically split hash ranges so membership changes move only a bounded share of keys.

theory.question: Fixed number of logical shards (many shards, fewer nodes): how it works and its limits
theory.answer:
Create many logical shards up front, then assign several of them to each physical node. Routing has two steps: hash the key to a logical shard, then look up which node currently owns that shard. Adding capacity moves whole logical shards and updates only the ownership map; records keep the same logical-shard identity.

This makes rebalancing predictable and supports heterogeneous machines by assigning more shards to stronger nodes. It also keeps the logical shard count stable while the node count changes.

The main limitation is that the initial shard count is a long-lived capacity decision. Too few shards cap future parallelism and make each move large; too many increase metadata, file, connection, and coordination overhead. A single hot key also remains hot because a logical shard cannot divide one key. Elasticsearch, Citus, Riak, and Couchbase use variants of this pattern.

theory.question: Hash-range sharding: combine hashing with dynamic range splits
theory.answer:
Hash-range sharding assigns each shard a contiguous range of hash values, not raw keys — getting even spread without fixing shard count upfront.

Downside vs raw key-range: range queries on the partition key scatter across all shards. Exception: composite keys where only the first column is the partition key — range queries on later columns stay within one shard if the prefix is fixed.

YugabyteDB, DynamoDB, and MongoDB offer hash-range style sharding.

Comment: This is the default mental model for DynamoDB — partition key hash determines the partition; sort key gives ordering inside the partition.

theory.question: Consistent hashing: properties and tradeoffs vs range splits
theory.answer:
Consistent hashing places both keys and shard owners in a hash space so a membership change remaps only the affected portion of that space. Virtual nodes or multiple tokens per owner improve balance; rendezvous and jump hashing provide related placement properties without maintaining the same ring structure.

The benefit is limited data movement when nodes join or leave. The costs are more complex routing, uneven ownership without enough tokens, and weaker locality for bulk transfer when a new owner receives scattered ranges.

Dynamic hash-range splitting is often easier for storage engines: each shard owns a contiguous interval of hash values, and an overloaded interval can split into two adjacent intervals. Consistent or rendezvous placement is attractive for caches and stateless routing; explicit ranges are attractive when operators need inspectable boundaries, streaming migration, and range-level metadata.

theory.question: Hot key / hot shard problem: causes and mitigation techniques
theory.answer:
A hot shard receives much more traffic than its peers; a hot key concentrates that traffic on one partition even when the overall key distribution is balanced.

Common causes include monotonically increasing range keys, celebrity accounts, viral posts, a small set of popular products, and low-cardinality secondary-index values. Measure requests, bytes, CPU, queue depth, and tail latency per shard and per key; cluster-wide averages hide the hotspot.

Mitigations depend on the access pattern. Add a nonmonotonic prefix to time-series keys, split one logical counter across suffix buckets, cache popular reads, replicate read-only hot data, rate-limit abusive clients, or isolate exceptional tenants. Splitting writes makes reads fan out and merge, so it should be targeted and reversible. Rebalancing an already saturated shard can add enough network and disk work to worsen the incident, which is why emergency moves need throttling and careful control.

theory.question:
Request routing to shards: three approaches, coordination with ZooKeeper/etcd, and solutions to shared hard problems:
- Who decides shard→node mapping, and how is the coordinator fault-tolerant without split brain?
- How do routers learn mapping changes?
- During shard migration, requests may still be in flight to the old node — need cutover handling.
theory.answer:
Request routing answers: given a key, which IP:port owns its shard?

Three approaches:
1. Contact any node (round-robin LB) — owner serves locally; otherwise forwards to the right node and relays the reply.
2. Dedicated routing tier (e.g., MongoDB `mongos`) — shard-aware load balancer that does not store data.
3. Shard-aware clients — connect directly to the correct node with no proxy.

Coordinator fault tolerance (who decides mapping, avoiding split brain):
- A small control plane holds the authoritative shard→node map — not individual data nodes and not DNS. Operators or an auto-rebalancer propose moves; only the coordinator commits them.
- The coordinator itself runs as a replicated quorum service (ZooKeeper ZAB, etcd Raft, MongoDB config-server replica set). Writes need a majority of replicas to ack, so a partitioned minority cannot publish a conflicting map — that is how split brain is avoided.
- Single-writer semantics: one elected leader applies mapping changes; followers replicate the log. Clients and routers read from any healthy replica but mutations go through the leader.
- Fencing with monotonic epochs: every mapping update carries a version/generation number (ZK zxid, etcd revision, MongoDB config version). Data nodes and routers reject or ignore assignments from a stale epoch — a zombie leader that lost quorum cannot overwrite a newer map.
- Data nodes register liveness (ephemeral ZK nodes, lease heartbeats). If a node is declared dead, the coordinator reassigns its shards only after the lease expires — avoids two nodes believing they own the same shard.
- Built-in Raft on data nodes (Kafka controller, YugabyteDB/TiDB placement driver, ScyllaDB) follows the same quorum rules without a separate ZK cluster.
- Riak gossip alternative: peers exchange mapping state without a central coordinator — simpler ops, weaker guarantees, possible divergent views tolerated because Riak already offers eventual consistency.

Comment: Vitess VTGate is another routing-tier example for MySQL sharding.

theory.question: Local vs global secondary indexes on a sharded database — write path, read path, and when to pick each
theory.answer:
A local secondary index is partitioned exactly like the primary table. Updating one row changes only its primary shard and that shard's index, so writes stay local. A query by the secondary attribute must contact every shard and combine the results because matching entries may exist anywhere.

A global secondary index is partitioned by the indexed value. The query can route directly to the relevant index shard, but a base-row write may update a different machine, creating distributed write amplification and a consistency problem between the table and index.

Choose local indexes for write-heavy OLTP when secondary queries are rare, narrow, or tolerant of scatter-gather. Choose global indexes when indexed lookups dominate and low read latency justifies the extra write path. For broad search and ranking, a separate search tier fed from the system of record is often clearer than adding many globally maintained indexes.

theory.question: Automatic vs manual shard rebalancing — tradeoffs and when a human should stay in the loop
theory.answer:
Automatic rebalancing reacts quickly and reduces routine operator work, but a controller can mistake temporary load, a slow dependency, or a partial outage for a permanent capacity change. Moving data consumes the same disk and network resources already under pressure, so an aggressive feedback loop can amplify the incident.

Manual rebalancing gives an operator context and control but responds slowly and is prone to inconsistent procedures. A hybrid is usually safer: the control plane computes a proposed assignment, estimates bytes and load, and requires approval for risky moves while allowing tightly bounded repairs automatically.

Throttle transfer bandwidth, limit concurrent moves, monitor replication lag and tail latency, and make ownership changes atomic. During a move, define how in-flight reads and writes reach the old and new owners. Disable or dampen automatic movement during known overload, then resume it after the cluster has spare capacity.

practice.task: [Python] Choose a partition key for IoT sensor readings — key-range vs hash-range
practice.question:
An IoT platform stores temperature readings that will later be sharded (Citus, DynamoDB, or an app router). Before picking a real shard key, simulate three partition strategies locally and measure write skew, query fan-out, and rebalance cost.

Workload model (encoded in the setup):
- 200 sensors, each writing once per second for 60 seconds (12,000 rows)
- All writes happen in the same calendar month (June 2026) — like live ingest
- Hot query A: all readings for sensor 42 in the simulated window
- Hot query B: all readings across all sensors on 2026-06-19 (daily rollup)

Strategies to compare:
- `recorded_at` only (monthly key-range)
- `sensor_id` only (hash of sensor_id)
- partition by `sensor_id`, keep `recorded_at` as a within-shard sort key (same routing as hash of sensor_id)

Prerequisites: Python 3.10+ (stdlib only; no pip packages required).

Save the file below as `ch7_iot_partition_keys.py`, then complete every function marked `# implement`. Run with `python3 ch7_iot_partition_keys.py`.

Expected signals after Tasks 1–4:
- monthly `recorded_at` key-range: `write_max` equals total rows and `write_min` is 0 (one hot shard)
- `sensor_id` hash: `write_max` / `write_min` skew well under 3, query A touches 1 shard, query B touches all 8 shards
- rebalance print shows most rows move when shard count goes 8 → 9 under plain `hash % N`
- final recommendation line names `sensor_id` as the partition key

```python
def print_report(

    vals = list(dist.values())
    mx, mn = max(vals), min(vals)

    print(f"write_max={mx} write_min={mn} skew_ratio={mx / max(mn, 1):.2f}")
```

Tasks:
1. Implement `shard_by_recorded_at`, `shard_by_sensor_id`, and `shard_by_sensor_then_time` at the `# implement` comments (monthly key-range vs hash on `sensor_id` vs partition-by-sensor with time as sort key only).
2. Implement `write_distribution`, `shards_for_query`, and `rebalance_on_add_shard` so `print_report` can measure skew, query A/B fan-out, and 8→9 shard moves.
3. Finish `main` so it prints the three reports, then prints `recommendation=partition_by_sensor_id_hash; sort_by_recorded_at_within_shard` and `query_B=serve_via_daily_rollup_or_analytics_store_not_oltp_scatter`.
4. Run `python3 ch7_iot_partition_keys.py` and confirm the expected signals above; note why plain `hash % N` rebalancing moves most rows when N changes.
practice.answer:
Use `sensor_id` as the partition key (hash-range) and sort by `recorded_at` within a shard. Monthly `recorded_at` key-range puts every live write on one hot shard. Query A stays single-shard with a sensor partition key; query B (all sensors, one day) is scatter-gather on the OLTP cluster — serve it from a daily rollup or analytics store. Plain `hash % N` rebalancing moves most rows when N changes (here ~90% on 8→9); production systems prefer fixed logical shards or consistent hashing so only whole shards move.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""ch7_iot_partition_keys.py — simulate partition-key choices for IoT readings."""
from __future__ import annotations

import hashlib
from collections import Counter
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from typing import Callable

NUM_SHARDS = 8
NUM_SENSORS = 200
SECONDS = 60
START = datetime(2026, 6, 19, 12, 0, tzinfo=timezone.utc)
QUERY_A_SENSOR = 42
QUERY_A_END = START + timedelta(seconds=SECONDS)
QUERY_B_DAY = START.date()


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Reading:
    sensor_id: int
    recorded_at: datetime
    value_c: float


def stable_hash(key: str) -> int:
    return int(hashlib.md5(key.encode()).hexdigest(), 16)


def make_workload() -> list[Reading]:
    rows: list[Reading] = []
    for sec in range(SECONDS):
        ts = START + timedelta(seconds=sec)
        for sid in range(NUM_SENSORS):
            rows.append(Reading(sid, ts, 20.0 + (sid % 5)))
    return rows


def shard_by_recorded_at(r: Reading, num_shards: int) -> int:
    month_ord = r.recorded_at.year * 12 + r.recorded_at.month
    return month_ord % num_shards


def shard_by_sensor_id(r: Reading, num_shards: int) -> int:
    return stable_hash(str(r.sensor_id)) % num_shards


def shard_by_sensor_then_time(r: Reading, num_shards: int) -> int:
    return shard_by_sensor_id(r, num_shards)


def write_distribution(
    rows: list[Reading], shard_fn: Callable[[Reading, int], int], num_shards: int
) -> dict[int, int]:
    counts: Counter[int] = Counter()
    for r in rows:
        counts[shard_fn(r, num_shards)] += 1
    return {i: counts.get(i, 0) for i in range(num_shards)}


def shards_for_query(
    rows: list[Reading],
    shard_fn: Callable[[Reading, int], int],
    num_shards: int,
    predicate: Callable[[Reading], bool],
) -> set[int]:
    touched: set[int] = set()
    for r in rows:
        if predicate(r):
            touched.add(shard_fn(r, num_shards))
    return touched


def rebalance_on_add_shard(
    rows: list[Reading],
    shard_fn: Callable[[Reading, int], int],
    old_n: int,
    new_n: int,
) -> int:
    moved = 0
    for r in rows:
        if shard_fn(r, old_n) != shard_fn(r, new_n):
            moved += 1
    return moved


def print_report(
    name: str, rows: list[Reading], shard_fn: Callable[[Reading, int], int]
) -> None:
    dist = write_distribution(rows, shard_fn, NUM_SHARDS)
    vals = list(dist.values())
    mx, mn = max(vals), min(vals)
    print(f"\n=== {name} ===")
    print(f"write_counts_per_shard: {dist}")
    print(f"write_max={mx} write_min={mn} skew_ratio={mx / max(mn, 1):.2f}")

    qa_pred = lambda r: (
        r.sensor_id == QUERY_A_SENSOR and START <= r.recorded_at < QUERY_A_END
    )
    qb_pred = lambda r: r.recorded_at.date() == QUERY_B_DAY
    qa = shards_for_query(rows, shard_fn, NUM_SHARDS, qa_pred)
    qb = shards_for_query(rows, shard_fn, NUM_SHARDS, qb_pred)
    print(f"query_A_shards={sorted(qa)} count={len(qa)}")
    print(f"query_B_shards={sorted(qb)} count={len(qb)}")

    moved = rebalance_on_add_shard(rows, shard_fn, NUM_SHARDS, NUM_SHARDS + 1)
    pct = 100.0 * moved / len(rows)
    print(f"rebalance_8_to_9_moved={moved} ({pct:.1f}% of rows)")


def main() -> None:
    rows = make_workload()
    print(f"workload_rows={len(rows)} sensors={NUM_SENSORS} shards={NUM_SHARDS}")
    print_report("recorded_at_monthly_key_range", rows, shard_by_recorded_at)
    print_report("sensor_id_hash", rows, shard_by_sensor_id)
    print_report("sensor_id_partition_recorded_at_sort", rows, shard_by_sensor_then_time)
    print("\nrecommendation=partition_by_sensor_id_hash; sort_by_recorded_at_within_shard")
    print("query_B=serve_via_daily_rollup_or_analytics_store_not_oltp_scatter")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Sample signals (12,000 rows, 8 shards):
- `recorded_at_monthly_key_range`: write_max=12000, write_min=0, query A/B both 1 shard (the hot month), rebalance 8→9 moves 100% of rows under `% N`
- `sensor_id_hash` / `sensor_id_partition_recorded_at_sort`: skew_ratio ≈ 1.6, query A count=1, query B count=8, rebalance 8→9 moves ~90% of rows

Comment: Prefixing the sensor ID before the timestamp prevents all current writes from landing on one time-range shard.

practice.task: [Python] Local vs global secondary indexes for a sharded used-car marketplace
practice.question:
A used-car marketplace shards listings by `listing_id` (hash of listing_id). Before picking MongoDB local vs global secondary indexes (or a search tier), simulate both strategies locally and measure which shards Q1–Q3 touch and how a price-drop update propagates.

Sample listing shape (for context only; the setup builds its own catalog):

```json
{ "_id": 742, "make": "Toyota", "color": "red", "price": 12000, "city": "Austin" }
```

Workload model (encoded in the setup):
- 4 primary shards; listings routed by `hash(listing_id) % 4`
- Catalog of mixed makes/colors/cities with several red cars under $15,000
- Q1: get listing by `_id` / `listing_id` (targeted primary lookup)
- Q2: all red cars with `price < 15000` (browse filter)
- Q3: all Toyota listings in Austin (`make` + `city`)
- Update U: drop price on listing 742 from 12000 to 11000

Index strategies:
- Local: each primary shard keeps secondary indexes only for its own listings (`color+price`, `make+city`)
- Global: term-partitioned indexes — `color` index keyed by color value; `make` index keyed by make (city filter applied after fetching postings)

Prerequisites: Python 3.10+ (stdlib only; no pip packages required).

Save the file below as `ch7_car_secondary_indexes.py`, then complete every function marked `# implement`. Run with `python3 ch7_car_secondary_indexes.py`.

Expected signals after Tasks 1–4:
- Q1 hits exactly 1 primary shard under both strategies
- Q2/Q3 under local indexes: `primary_shards` count equals 4 (scatter-gather)
- Q2 under global: `index_shards` count equals 1 (the `red` term shard); primary fetch count is only shards that own matching red listings
- Q3 under global: `index_shards` count equals 1 (the `Toyota` term shard)
- price-drop U local: `shards_touched=1` (primary only)
- price-drop U global: `shards_touched>=2` (primary + at least the color index shard)
- final recommendation names local indexes for OLTP + a search/analytics tier for hot browse filters like Q2

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""ch7_car_secondary_indexes.py — local vs global secondary indexes on sharded listings."""
from __future__ import annotations

import hashlib
from collections import defaultdict
from dataclasses import dataclass

NUM_PRIMARY = 4
NUM_INDEX = 4
PRICE_CAP = 15000
TARGET_ID = 742


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Listing:
    listing_id: int
    make: str
    color: str
    price: int
    city: str


def stable_hash(key: str) -> int:
    return int(hashlib.md5(key.encode()).hexdigest(), 16)


def make_catalog() -> list[Listing]:
    # Deterministic mini catalog: ids span all primary shards; includes Q2/Q3 hits.
    rows = [
        Listing(100, "Honda", "blue", 9000, "Dallas"),
        Listing(250, "Toyota", "red", 14000, "Austin"),
        Listing(401, "Ford", "red", 8000, "Houston"),
        Listing(520, "Toyota", "silver", 16000, "Austin"),
        Listing(742, "Toyota", "red", 12000, "Austin"),
        Listing(803, "BMW", "black", 22000, "Austin"),
        Listing(910, "Toyota", "red", 14999, "Dallas"),
        Listing(999, "Honda", "red", 15500, "Austin"),
```

practice.answer:
Consistent hashing with 128 vnodes per node moves only ~26% of keys on 3→4 and 4→3. Add migrations all go to `node-d`; remove migrations all leave `node-d`. Migration entries use `{key, from, to}`. Invalidate `_key_cache` on every ring mutation. Operational cutover keeps the old assignment serving traffic while batches copy `(from, to)` with rate limits (book: old assignment used during transfer). Human-approve rebalance near max throughput.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""ch7_consistent_hashing.py — consistent hashing ring with vnode rebalance plans."""
from __future__ import annotations

import bisect
import hashlib
from collections import defaultdict
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

KEYS = [f"key-{i:05d}" for i in range(10_000)]
VNODE_COUNT = 128
NODES_3 = ["node-a", "node-b", "node-c"]
NODES_4 = NODES_3 + ["node-d"]


def stable_hash(key: str) -> int:
    return int(hashlib.md5(key.encode()).hexdigest(), 16)


@dataclass
class HashRing:
    vnode_count: int = VNODE_COUNT
    _positions: list[int] = field(default_factory=list)
    _owners: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    _key_cache: dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)

    def _insert_vnodes(self, node: str) -> None:
        for i in range(self.vnode_count):
            pos = stable_hash(f"{node}#{i}")
            idx = bisect.bisect(self._positions, pos)
            self._positions.insert(idx, pos)
            self._owners.insert(idx, node)

    def _remove_vnodes(self, node: str) -> None:
        for i in reversed([i for i, o in enumerate(self._owners) if o == node]):
            del self._positions[i]
            del self._owners[i]

    def build(self, nodes: list[str]) -> None:
        self._positions.clear()
        self._owners.clear()
        self._key_cache.clear()
        for node in sorted(nodes):
            self._insert_vnodes(node)

    def get_node(self, key: str) -> str:
        if key in self._key_cache:
            return self._key_cache[key]
        if not self._positions:
            raise RuntimeError("ring is empty")
        idx = bisect.bisect(self._positions, stable_hash(key)) % len(self._positions)
        self._key_cache[key] = self._owners[idx]
        return self._key_cache[key]

    def _diff(self, keys: list[str], before: dict[str, str]) -> list[dict]:
        self._key_cache.clear()
        plan = []
        for k in keys:
            new_owner = self.get_node(k)
            if before[k] != new_owner:
                plan.append({"key": k, "from": before[k], "to": new_owner})
        return plan

    def add_node(self, node: str, keys: list[str]) -> list[dict]:
        before = {k: self.get_node(k) for k in keys}
        self._insert_vnodes(node)
        return self._diff(keys, before)

    def remove_node(self, node: str, keys: list[str]) -> list[dict]:
        before = {k: self.get_node(k) for k in keys}
        self._remove_vnodes(node)
        if not self._positions:
            raise RuntimeError("cannot remove last node")
        return self._diff(keys, before)


def print_batches(label: str, plan: list[dict]) -> None:
    batches: dict[tuple[str, str], int] = defaultdict(int)
    for m in plan:
        batches[(m["from"], m["to"])] += 1
    print(f"\n=== {label}: {len(plan)} keys ({100 * len(plan) / len(KEYS):.1f}%) ===")
    for (src, dst), n in sorted(batches.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1]):
        print(f"  {src} → {dst}: {n}")


def main() -> None:
    # --- ADD: 3 → 4 ---
    ring = HashRing()
    ring.build(NODES_3)
    add_plan = ring.add_node("node-d", KEYS)

    print("=== rebalance cost: ADD 3 → 4 ===")
    print(f"consistent hash: {len(add_plan):5d} keys")
    print_batches("add migrations", add_plan)
    assert all(m["to"] == "node-d" for m in add_plan)

    # --- REMOVE: 4 → 3 (node-d failed) ---
    ring2 = HashRing()
    ring2.build(NODES_4)
    rem_plan = ring2.remove_node("node-d", KEYS)

    print("\n=== rebalance cost: REMOVE 4 → 3 (drop node-d) ===")
    print(f"consistent hash: {len(rem_plan):5d} keys")
    print_batches("remove migrations", rem_plan)

    # On remove, only ex-node-d keys should move
    assert all(m["from"] == "node-d" for m in rem_plan)
    assert len(rem_plan) == len(add_plan)  # symmetric for same vnode layout


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Sample signals (10k keys, 128 vnodes):
- ADD 3→4: 2607 keys (26.1%); all migrations `to=node-d` (e.g. node-b→node-d 1118, node-c→node-d 898, node-a→node-d 591)
- REMOVE 4→3: 2607 keys (26.1%); all migrations `from=node-d` (symmetric reverse batches)

Key insight on remove: only keys whose clockwise successor vnode belonged to the removed node move. Keys already on a/b/c never move.

Comment: Cassandra token removal and Dynamo vnode decommission follow this same migration-plan pattern.

practice.question:
A social app shards by `post_id` (hash-range). Celebrity post `post_id = 9001` receives a viral burst: comment writes and comment-count reads concentrate on one shard while other shards stay idle. Workload model (encoded in the setup):
- 8 shards; routing is `hash(key) % 8` with a stable MD5 hash
- Viral window: 1,000 comment writes on `post_id=9001`
- Plain path: every write hits key `"9001"` (one hot shard)
- Split path: round-robin writes across `"9001#00"` … `"9001#09"` (10 suffixes)
- Reads: serve `comment_count` from an in-process cache when present; otherwise fan-out-sum the suffix keys
- Cooldown: merge suffix buckets back into `"9001"`, then clear suffixes
- Rebalance: refuse automatic shard split while the viral flag is on

practice.task: [PostgreSQL] Protect a shared multi-tenant table with row-level security
practice.question:
Prerequisites: Docker Engine 24+ (or Docker Desktop). No local PostgreSQL installation is required.

```bash
# Start the pre-seeded lab (database ch7_rls_lab)
docker run -d --name lab-ch7-p7 -p 5432:5432 ghcr.io/anmisttt/lab:ch7-p7

# Copy the starter file setup.sql into the current directory

# Interactive session. The lab connects as postgres, a superuser that can create
# roles and schemas — this exercise needs both.

# Apply setup.sql; re-run after each edit (it recreates the schema and its rows)
docker exec -i lab-ch7-p7 psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U postgres -d ch7_rls_lab < setup.sql

# Teardown

```

A shared-table SaaS stores projects for Acme and Globex in one PostgreSQL table. The application currently relies on handwritten tenant filters, and the starter schema has no database-enforced tenant isolation or application access model. Implement PostgreSQL row-level security and least-privilege role access from scratch, then carry tenant context only for the current transaction.

The `ch7_rls_lab` database already contains the starter schema and both rows. `init` copies the same statements as `setup.sql`, which creates only the schema, table, and sample rows — role separation, privileges, RLS, and policies are intentionally absent, and implementing all of them is part of the exercise. Because `setup.sql` drops and rebuilds the schema, it also reinserts the two seed rows, so re-applying it always returns you to a known state:

```sql
-- setup.sql
DROP SCHEMA IF EXISTS rls_lab CASCADE;
CREATE SCHEMA rls_lab;

CREATE TABLE rls_lab.projects (
  id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY,
  tenant_id uuid NOT NULL,
  name text NOT NULL,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, id),
  UNIQUE (tenant_id, name)
);

INSERT INTO rls_lab.projects (tenant_id, name) VALUES
  ('11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111', 'Alpha project'),
  ('22222222-2222-2222-2222-222222222222', 'Beta project');
```

Before implementing access control, run this baseline query in the `psql` session above. It demonstrates that the shared table itself does not isolate tenants: an unfiltered query sees both rows.

```sql
SELECT
  array_agg(name ORDER BY name) AS visible_projects,
  count(DISTINCT tenant_id) AS visible_tenants
FROM rls_lab.projects;
```

Expected baseline signal: `visible_projects` contains Alpha project and Beta project, and `visible_tenants=2`.

A GUI client such as DBeaver is optional; if you use one, keep the test statements in a single SQL console and use explicit transactions, because the tenant context in task 5 is transaction-local.

Tasks:
1. Apply the starter file and run the baseline query. Confirm that an unfiltered administrator query sees both tenants and that the starter contains no database authorization boundary.
2. Extend the file with a non-login role that owns the schema objects and a separate login role for application queries. The application role must not own the table, must not be a superuser, and must not have `BYPASSRLS`. Make the setup re-runnable by safely dropping and recreating the lab roles and schema in a valid dependency order.
3. Implement least-privilege access for the application role. It needs to use the schema, read and modify projects, and obtain values from the identity sequence, but it must not own the objects or receive schema-creation or policy-management privileges.
4. Enable and force row-level security on `rls_lab.projects`. Create a policy for the application role whose `USING` and `WITH CHECK` expressions compare the row's `tenant_id` with `NULLIF(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')::uuid`. Explain which operations `USING` controls and which new row values `WITH CHECK` validates.
5. Re-apply the completed file. As the application role, set tenant A inside `BEGIN` with transaction-local `set_config(..., true)`. Confirm an unfiltered `SELECT` returns only Alpha project, then attempt to insert a tenant B row and confirm PostgreSQL rejects it with a row-level security policy error.
6. Inspect `current_user`, `session_user`, `rolsuper`, and `rolbypassrls`. Confirm no tenant context returns zero rows; confirm `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` subjects the table owner to default-deny because the owner has no applicable policy; then observe that the administrator still sees both rows. Commit a transaction that set tenant A locally, verify the setting is cleared and an unfiltered application query returns zero rows, and explain the implications for GUI-client auto-commit, pooled connections, and deriving tenant identity from verified authentication.
